cf.title: Improve row mark handling in self-join elimination

input.subject: Self-join elimination discards differing row lock wait policies

verdict_reasoning: Only demand-1 survived, and it applies to 0002 alone. The thread shows no user query that self-joins one table with different lock strengths per alias, and message #7 does not answer Tom Lane's doubt in message #4 that the merging is worth the trouble. 0001 removes unreachable code and expands comments, and no objection to it survived. The verdict rests on missing evidence of demand, so confidence is low.

brief.title: Clean up row mark handling in self-join elimination and merge lock strengths
brief.problem: The thread started as a bug report: SJE drops one wait policy when two aliases use NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED. Tom Lane argued this is not a reachable bug, and the author agreed. What remains is unreachable code and thin comments in analyzejoins.c, and the fact that differing lock strengths block SJE, so the outcome depends on join order and the weaker lock taken first can deadlock on upgrade.
brief.proposed_design: 0001 removes the unreachable code that moves the removed relation's row mark when the kept relation has none, adds assertions for the invariant, and expands comments. 0002 lets SJE merge locking row marks of different strengths. It keeps the stronger lock and its wait policy, and for equal strengths keeps the stronger wait policy, as applyLockingClause() does.
user_visible_surface: Plan change: queries with FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE variants of different strength on two self-joined aliases can now get self-join elimination.
author_claims: preprocess_rowmarks() gives every non-target base relation a row mark when any are needed, so SJE candidates either both have marks or both lack them.
Merging into the stronger lock avoids the lock-upgrade deadlock risk of taking the weaker lock first.
The original NOWAIT versus SKIP LOCKED example is not a correctness bug.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane analyzed the case, shared a WIP patch that 0002 builds on, and doubted the strength merging is worth the trouble. No one has reviewed v3, and a separate idea about constant-restricted self-joins was judged mostly cosmetic.
unclear: Whether Tom Lane accepts 0002 now that much of his WIP code proved unreachable.
Whether choosing the stronger wait policy across different lock strengths matches the semantics of a legal non-SJE plan in every case.
Whether 0002 is meant for back branches or master only.
What the new regression tests in join.sql cover.

prior_attempts.title: Revert: Remove useless self-joins
prior_attempts.quote: We are quite late in the release cycle and new bugs continue to appear.
prior_attempts.reason:
This commit reverts d3d55ce5713 and subsequent fixes 2b26a694554, 93c85db3b5b,
b44a1708abe, b7f315c9d7d, 8a8ed916f73, b5fb6736ed3, 0a93f803f45, e0477837ce4,
a7928a57b9f, 5ef34a8fc38, 30b4955a466, 8c441c08279, 028b15405b4, fe093994db4,
489072ab7a9, and 466979ef031.

We are quite late in the release cycle and new bugs continue to appear.  Even
though we have fixes for all known bugs, there is a risk of throwing many
bugs to end users.

The plan for self-join elimination would be to do more review and testing,
then re-commit in the early v18 cycle.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 reverted the whole self-join elimination feature late in a release cycle because bugs kept appearing. This proposal is a narrow change to row mark handling in the re-committed feature, and 0001 only removes code.

objections.title: No user is shown writing self-joins with differing lock strengths
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes 0002, which adds merge logic to the row-mark handling in analyzejoins.c, an area where SJE bugs have been found. Later fixes to that logic cost committer time and may need backpatching. The thread names no query that gains from the change, so the payoff for that cost is not known.
objections.argument: The only queries in the thread come from developers: message #1's example uses equal strengths, and its supposed bug was withdrawn in message #5. Tom Lane raised strength merging as a possible improvement in message #3, then wrote in message #4 that he was 'not really convinced that it's worth the trouble'. Message #7 does not answer that doubt; it ports his WIP code. The deadlock-on-upgrade argument is sound in principle, but no report shows a user who hit it.
objections.author_must_show: Which real applications or ORMs emit self-joins on a unique key with different FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE strengths per alias, and has anyone reported the lock-upgrade deadlock?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows no user query with mixed lock strengths on self-joined aliases, and message #7 does not answer Tom Lane's doubt in message #4. The deadlock and join-order points in message #3 give a motive but no evidence of demand.

refuted.title: Lock-strength merging in SJE adds planner code with no shown demand
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer takes 0002 to support self-joined aliases with different FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE strengths, a query shape no user has reported. Later a bug in the merge silently changes which lock or wait policy a query uses. Users see it as an unexpected skip, block or error under concurrency, long after commit.
refuted.argument: In message #4 Tom Lane, who knows this code, said he was not convinced lock-strength merging is worth the trouble, and he stopped his WIP once preprocess_rowmarks made much of it unreachable (message #6). The thread came from a non-bug, and no field report asks for this case. SJE already has a record of fragility: [P2] was reverted because new bugs kept appearing. 0001 stands alone and can go in first. 0002 fits a "not now, show demand" outcome.
refuted.author_must_show: Which real applications self-join one table under different row lock strengths, and what do they hit today without 0002?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1. [P2] records a late-cycle revert of the whole SJE feature, which was planned for re-commit, so it must not be used as support against 0002.

refuted.title: Second copy of the locking-clause merge rule outside applyLockingClause
refuted.failure_scenario: A future patch adds a lock strength or wait policy, or changes how applyLockingClause() combines them. It updates the parser path and not analyzejoins.c. SJE plans then merge row marks by the old rule, and nothing fails until a user sees different locking with SJE on and off.
refuted.argument: The 0002 commit message says the wait-policy rule follows applyLockingClause(), so the same rule would then live in two places. The prose does not say whether 0002 shares a helper with applyLockingClause() or copies its logic. A copied rule has no test or assertion that fails when the two diverge.
refuted.author_must_show: Does 0002 call a helper shared with applyLockingClause(), so a change to the merge rule cannot reach one path and miss the other?

critic.reasoning: applyLockingClause() combines by Max() over ordered enums, so a new value placed in order reaches any comparison-based copy. By message #3, the SJE rule only needs to match a legal non-SJE plan, so drift from the parser is not a failure.

refuted.title: Users can already get SJE by writing one lock strength on both aliases
refuted.failure_scenario: A user who writes `for update of p for share of q` on a self-join can change it to `for update of p, q` today and get SJE with one lock. With 0002, core keeps a merge rule for lock strengths and wait policies across different strengths. Every future change to SJE row mark handling must keep that rule correct.
refuted.argument: The existing path already works: matching locking clauses on both aliases give equal markType, and SJE goes ahead. 0002 only helps queries that mix strengths on two aliases of the same row, and the thread shows no user who writes such queries. In message #4 Tom Lane doubted the merging is worth the trouble. Message #3 gives the join-order dependence and the deadlock risk as the reasons, but the user can remove both by writing one strength.
refuted.author_must_show: Which applications or ORMs emit different lock strengths on two aliases of the same table, and why can they not emit one strength?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1. The rewrite argument applies to all of SJE, since a user can always remove the self-join by hand, so it adds nothing beyond the demand question.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: 0002 lets self-join elimination apply when two aliases carry locking row marks of different strength, so those plans change.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The thread does not say whether 0002, a plan and locking behaviour change, targets master only.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: 0002 adds a merge rule for lock strength and wait policy to the row mark handling in analyzejoins.c.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which real applications or ORMs emit self-joins on a unique key with different FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE strengths per alias, and has anyone reported the lock-upgrade deadlock?
When the two aliases differ in both lock strength and wait policy, does the merged row mark always behave like some legal join order of the plan without self-join elimination?
Is 0002 meant for master only, and is 0001 meant to be committed alone if 0002 waits?
Which combinations of lock strength and wait policy do the new tests in join.sql cover?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane analyzed the case and wrote the WIP patch that 0002 builds on, but he has not reviewed v3 and doubted in message #4 that 0002 is worth it. The owner needs to know planner row marks and self-join elimination.
committability.liability: For 0001, the new assertions that preprocess_rowmarks() gives both candidates a row mark or neither. For 0002, the correctness of merged lock strength and wait policy under concurrency, for as long as self-join elimination exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author revised the patch to v3 after agreeing with the committer's analysis and created the CommitFest entry. There is no explicit statement about post-commit fixes.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: For 0002: a field report, a -general or -bugs thread, or an ORM-generated query that self-joins a table with different lock strengths per alias and hits the lock-upgrade deadlock or join-order dependence. A statement from Tom Lane that he now wants the merging would also change it. 0001 needs no such evidence.

priority.reason: 0001 is a small cleanup in one file that follows the committer's own analysis and can go ahead alone. 0002 is also small but serves a query shape no user has reported, so it should wait for evidence of demand.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check that the assertions in 0001 hold for every path into self-join elimination. I also could not check that the merge rule in 0002 matches a legal plan without self-join elimination for every pair of strength and wait policy.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove ctid from self-join examples in UPDATE and DELETE docs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the self-join examples in the UPDATE and DELETE docs to join on an id column, not ctid. The author argues that a ctid self-join behaves like a join on a mutable column under concurrent updates, so readers could copy it to avoid deadlocks and lose updates without notice.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Only the author's first message is shown, with no replies, and the entry was later withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document efficient self-joins / UPDATE LIMIT techniques.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds documentation examples that show how to update or delete rows in batches, using a CTE with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and `LIMIT` and a self-join on the system column `ctid`. It offers this as a documented workaround while `UPDATE` and `DELETE` have no `LIMIT` clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because Laurenz Albe's review comments were not yet resolved. His comments covered redundant examples, the stated rationale and wording. Corey Huinker then sent a revised patch, and Laurenz Albe judged it close to ready for committer. The author had reopened the entry in the commitfest that was already closed, so Laurenz Albe closed it again and moved the patch to a new entry in the open commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow self-conflicting INSERT INTO .. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATEs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE accept a command whose own proposed rows conflict with each other, as DO NOTHING already does. Today such a command fails with "command cannot affect row a second time".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Peter Geoghegan voted against it, and the CFM returned it citing those two votes. Andres Freund objected that the patch makes one command update a row it inserted, producing cmin == cmax and breaking heap visibility rules. The author then found visibility bugs in his own patch. Peter Geoghegan argued that updating the same row twice in one command is not desirable and asked who would want it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To me it seems as if allowing the same command to update the same row more than once is just not desirable in general.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow multiple recursive self-references
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the recursive term of a `with recursive` query reference the CTE more than once, with all references reading the same working table, while still allowing only linear recursion. It also rotates the UNION parse tree in parse analysis so that non-recursive and recursive branches can appear in any order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane's review found that the patch appears to break rewriteSearchAndCycle(), which assumes a recursive query is a UNION of exactly two SELECTs. He also found the tree-rotation and checkWellFormedSelectStmt changes undercommented and was not convinced the new loop terminates. Peter Eisentraut accepted the semantics and executor changes but still disputed the parse-analysis rewrite and would not commit without another reviewer. No author reply follows Tom Lane's review, and the entry was closed after waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Doesn't it break rewriteSearchAndCycle() completely?  That code assumes (without a lot of checking) that a recursive query is a UNION [ALL] of exactly two SELECTs.

precedents_retrieved.title: Self contradictory examining on rel's baserestrictinfo
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a separate planner pass that examines a relation's baserestrictinfo for self-contradictory quals (btree strategy operators, <>, NULL tests, boolean tests, ScalarArrayOp and row comparisons) and marks the relation dummy. The pass also simplifies redundant quals, such as reducing a <= 10 and a = 10 to a = 10.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Much of the contradiction detection already exists through constraint_exclusion = on and predtest.c, and Tom Lane questioned whether the remaining cases are common enough to justify the added planner cycles. He asked the author to integrate the work with predtest.c and indxpath.c, and not to add a separate analysis pass of a few thousand lines. The patch also lacked comments and changed existing regression tests in ways that would need analysis. Tom Lane returned it because he did not expect anything close to it to be committed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So in short, my main review comment is that you should be looking
to integrate with existing planner functionality such as predtest.c
and indxpath.c, rather than writing a few thousand lines of
not-connected-to-anything-else code.  It's too hard to make the
case that these optimizations are worth the cost if they require
an entire separate analysis pass.

precedents_retrieved.title: Redundant qualifier elimination
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner drop a base-relation restriction clause when an equal() clause is already present, so a qual repeated in a JOIN's ON clause and the WHERE clause is not counted twice in selectivity. The check sits in add_base_clause_to_rel() and handles only identical quals.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane opposed the patch even with fixes, because it adds roughly O(N^2) planning cost in the number of restriction clauses to every query in order to handle badly written queries. Denis Smirnov showed that removing a duplicate volatile clause such as nextval('s') = 1 changes query results, and that the patch does not fix the JIT regression in the original report. The author accepted the feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It would impose nontrivial
costs on every query --- roughly O(N^2) in the number of restriction
clauses --- in order to fix badly-written queries, and that is not
a tradeoff I like.

precedents_retrieved.title: LockHasWaiters() crashes on fast-path locks
precedents_retrieved.summary: LockHasWaiters() dereferences NULL lock and proclock pointers when the LOCALLOCK was taken via the fast path, which crashes for weak lock modes such as AccessShareLock. Early versions moved the lock into the main lock table first; v4 instead searches LockMethodProcLockHash and returns false when no entry exists.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier saw no reason to support the case on its own, because no core caller or test needs it; the only existing caller uses AccessExclusiveLock, which is never fast-pathed. He suggested an assert and a comment instead, and said the patch looks like dead code without the separate autoprewarm proposal that needs it. Bharath Rupireddy withdrew the entry and moved the patch into the autoprewarm thread as 0001.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see a strong need to support this case if we have nothing in core to test it and nothing in core that needs it, and there are no facts that we need to do anything.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove LEFT JOINs in more cases
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner remove a LEFT JOIN whose inner relation is unused even when the join can duplicate rows, if a DISTINCT or a GROUP BY without aggregates removes those duplicates again. It adds this check in join_is_removable() next to the existing unique-index and subquery proofs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Antonin Houska's review found that the volatility checks miss some cases. A volatile function in a DISTINCT ON expression is not detected. The check of brel->lateral_vars does not look at the actual variables, so a lateral function referencing both sides of the join is not handled. The author returned the patch himself because the commitfest had no time left to address the review.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit 462bd95705a0c23ba0b0ba60a78d32566a0384c1, I changed postgres_fdw
to rely on get_plan_rowmark() instead of get_parse_rowmark().  I still
think that's a good idea in the long run, but as Etsuro Fujita pointed out,
it doesn't work today because planner.c forces PlanRowMarks to have
markType = ROW_MARK_COPY for all foreign tables.  There's no urgent reason
to change this in the back branches, so let's just revert that part of
yesterday's commit rather than trying to design a better solution under
time pressure.

Also, add a regression test case showing what postgres_fdw does with FOR
UPDATE/SHARE.  I'd blithely assumed there was one already, else I'd have
realized yesterday that this code didn't work.

roaster_notes.note: The only precedent, [P2], reverted the whole SJE feature because of late-cycle bug risk, and that reason does not carry over to a small row mark change posted early in a cycle. The thread points to no earlier attempt at merging lock strengths, apart from the WIP patch in message #6. Tom Lane's doubt about whether 0002 is worth it (message #4) is a desirability question for the other angles.

No objection from the standards and compatibility angle. 0002 adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object or dump content. The visible change is that some queries with locking clauses of different strength on two self-joined aliases now get self-join elimination. Per Tom Lane's argument in message #3, the merged lock strength and wait policy still behave like a legal non-SJE join order. The rule also matches the existing rule for repeated locking clauses on one table in applyLockingClause(), and enable_self_join_elimination remains an escape hatch. Points not checkable from the material: whether 0002 is meant for master only, since a plan change in a minor release would be unwelcome; and whether the SELECT locking-clause documentation should say that the strongest-clause rule now also covers aliases merged by SJE. The precedent [P2] concerns the revert of SJE as a whole for late-cycle bug risk, so it does not apply to this contract question.

Both patches change only planner logic in analyzejoins.c plus regression tests. They add no catalog column, WAL record, on-disk format, wire message or struct change. The row locks taken are ordinary tuple locks under existing rules, and FOR UPDATE is not allowed on a hot standby, so this angle finds nothing persistent or cross-node to object to.

No security objection. The merged lock is a strength the same query already asked for on the same table, so Postgres checked the needed privilege at parse time and no user gets a lock or data they could not get before. The proposal adds no new privilege, default or exposure. Not checked without the code: whether a view-derived alias with a different permission owner keeps its own checks.
0001 (dead code removal, assertions, comments) has no objection from this angle and follows Tom Lane's analysis in message #4.
0001 is a cleanup of unreachable code and comments, and no existing feature or extension replaces it. The only objection from this angle concerns 0002.
0001 is a cleanup of unreachable code and comments that Tom Lane asked for, so it needs no evidence of demand. The objection applies to 0002 only.
